question: What authority did the Ambassadors' Conference cite in March 1923 when awarding Vilna to Poland?
answer: The Ambassadors' Conference derived its authority from Article 87 of the Treaty of Versailles, which stipulates that the boundaries of Poland not laid down in the Treaty will be subsequently determined by the Principal Allied and Associated Powers.

question: Why did Britain care so much about a frontier in the Middle East in the 1920s?
answer: Britain's concern stemmed from its mandate over Iraq and the belief that the Mosul vilayet was economically and strategically essential to Iraq's viability, including its potential oil resources and agricultural wealth, as well as Britain's broader imperial interests in the region as a link to India and the East.

evidence.passage: You cannot develop Iraq into anything that will maintain itself and help the Empire with markets—because I look at both aspects—unless it includes the Mosul area. Its revenues will not be sufficient. Its economic production will not be of an order to make itself sufficiently maintain its population.

That was the question of the future of Mosul, a point to which the Turks attached enormous importance, but the importance of which to us could not be for a moment denied, because of its necessity to the mandated territory of Mesopotamia, or, as it is now called, Iraq, which we were responsible for having set up.

question: Why couldn't Turkey and Britain just agree on the border themselves?
answer: Direct negotiations between Britain and Turkey over the Mosul frontier repeatedly failed to reach agreement, so the matter was referred to the League of Nations for a binding decision, with both parties agreeing to accept the League Council's ruling.

evidence.passage: The question of the Turco-Iraq frontier was referred to the Council of the League of Nations in accordance with Article 3 (2) of the Treaty of Lausanne. As a result, it has beers agreed at Geneva that the Council will delimit the frontier between Turkey and Iraq, and both the Turkish and British delegates have given undertakings that their respective Governments will accept any decision which the Council may adopt and will meanwhile maintain and respect the status quo, that is to say, the position as it stood at the time of the conclusion of the Treaty of Lausanne.

As regards Mosul, instead of fighting it out there—although we did discuss it at the table—instead of trying to find a solution there, we agreed to remit the matter to negotiations between the two Powers, and these negotiations are about to begin at Constantinople. If they are unsuccessful, then we provide in the Treaty for the reference of the matter to the League of Nations.

question: Was oil the real reason behind the Mosul dispute?
answer: This was hotly disputed in Parliament. Critics like Thurtle, Wallhead, and Kenworthy argued oil was the real motive behind British policy, while Sir Austen Chamberlain strongly denied this, pointing out that Britain had rejected a Turkish offer in March 1925 that would have given Britain all the oil concessions in exchange for ceding most of Mosul to Turkey.

evidence.passage: If we were after oil, we could have had a concession for all the oil in Mosul and concessions for anything else we liked. The reply of His Majesty's Government was that they were trustees for Iraq; that they were not possessors, but mandatories, and that as mandatories and trustees they could not bargain away the rights and interests of Iraq and her people in exchange for concessions to British capitalists. There never was a shameful allegation made with less shadow of foundation.
It is said that Mosul has nothing whatever to do with oil. I want to ask one question. Assume for a moment that Mosul was a cabbage patch. Would you be there? You would not be there at all.

question: What did the people living in the disputed area actually want?
answer: Accounts conflicted: some MPs who visited reported the local population strongly welcomed British rule and the League's decision, fearing a return of Turkish rule, while others argued the population was split, with many families divided between pro-Turk and pro-British sentiment due to fear of Turkish vengeance.

evidence.passage: I had the privilege of talking to a very great many, not only of the big men in the country, but to the small men, and all over, and on every side I found an intense desire for the British occupation and the British lead to establish Iraq on a, firm basis extended from one side of the country to the other side.

When we got there, we found that 50 per cent. of the members of the large families were pro-Turk and the other 56 per cent. were pro-British. The reason for that was simply fear of the return of the Turk—fear of the vengeance of the Turk if by any chance he returned.

question: Why did the League fail to get Poland out of Vilna?
answer: The League of Nations was not able to force Poland out of Vilna; instead, responsibility for deciding Vilna's fate was ultimately handed to the Ambassadors' Conference, which decided in Poland's favor using authority from the Treaty of Versailles rather than any League mandate. The League had asked the parties to accept proposed conditions, but Poland and Lithuania rejected those terms, so the matter reverted to the Allied Powers who awarded Vilna to Poland.

The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative. The Ambassadors' Conference derives the authority to take such a decision from Article 87 of the Treaty of Versailles, which stipulates that the boundaries of Poland not laid down in the Treaty will be subsequently determined by the Principal Allied and Associated Powers.

question: Why did the League fail there?
answer: The League's Vilna Commission could not even secure an armistice, as Polish irregular forces under General Zeligowski (disowned by the Polish government) kept attacking the Lithuanians despite the League's involvement, and when the League later tried to mediate a settlement by proposing conditions, both Poland and Lithuania rejected the terms, so the League's role effectively ended and the dispute was resolved instead by the Ambassadors' Conference awarding Vilna to Poland under Treaty of Versailles authority.

question: Which disputes did the League of Nations manage to settle in the early 1920s?
answer: The League of Nations handled the Aaland Islands dispute between Sweden and Finland, successfully referring it to a commission and Council for settlement; it also handled the Mosul/Iraq-Turkey frontier dispute, with a Commission investigating and the Council ultimately delimiting the frontier; and it was involved in the Polish-Lithuanian dispute over Vilna, though with less success in fully resolving it.

evidence.passage: As stated by hon. Friend the Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs on the 23rd June, in reply to a question by my hon. Friend the Member for Lincoln, the Secretary of State, acting in exercise of the friendly right conferred by Article XI. of the Covenant of the League of Nations, has brought to the attention of the Council of the League the case of the Aaland Islands as a matter affecting international relations, which unfortunately threatens to disturb the good understanding between nations upon whom peace depends. He has informed the Governments of Sweden and Finland of the action which he felt it his duty to take, and both Governments have expressed their satisfaction that the case will now be examined without delay.

There is no tribunal in Brussels, as suggested. Monsieur Hymans has been delegated by the League of Nations to preside over conferences between Polish and Lithuanian delegates in Brussels, and will submit any solution that may be reached to the Council of the League of Nations for its decision.

question: Which disputes involved Poland, and how did they turn out?
answer: Poland was involved in the Upper Silesia plebiscite dispute with Germany, which was eventually handled through negotiations and an economic convention with a League-appointed chairman presiding over the mixed commission; and in the Polish-Lithuanian dispute over Vilna, which Poland effectively resolved in its favor through the Ambassadors' Conference awarding Vilna to Poland under Article 87 of the Treaty of Versailles, bypassing a full League of Nations decision after Lithuania and Poland rejected League-devised terms.

question: How quickly did the League act when fighting broke out on the Greek-Bulgarian border, and why did it work?
